subsystem: Purchase cycle — vendors, purchase bills, purchase credit/debit notes, purchase payments, TDS on purchase (resident + §195), ITC capture and reversal, vendor statements, MSME tracker, expense capture / document intelligence for bills
what_exists:
Backend. `routers/purchase_bills.py` (1930 lines) is the centre: `_compute_bill_lines_and_totals` computes per-line GST in integer paise (full tax then split CGST/SGST so it equals the IGST a supply would attract), aggregates §17(5) blocked credit into header `ineligible_itc_*_paise`, converts to base INR via `domain/currency/document_currency`, then resolves TDS. TDS routes by RESIDENCY first: `domain/tds/residency.py` says the 194-series charges only sums paid "to a resident", so a non-resident vendor goes to `domain/tds/section_195.py` (chargeability → nature → §90(2) treaty → §206AA/Rule 37BC → surcharge + cess), and a resident goes to `domain/tds/tds_computer.resolve_tds` over the FY-versioned `domain/tds/section_rates.py`. Endpoints: list, create, `POST /bulk` (pre-fetched vendor/client cache, dedup, per-row errors), get, `GET /{id}/document-url` (signed URL minted on demand), delete (draft-only hard delete), PATCH (draft = full recompute; received = `_SOFT_BILL_UPDATE_FIELDS` only), `POST /{id}/receive` (journal via the one kernel, status rollback on posting failure, `_sync_tds_register`, inventory stock-in), `POST /{id}/cancel` (append-only kernel reversal + register removal + stock reversal), and `POST /from-document`.

`routers/purchase_payments.py` records single-bill or unlinked vendor payments with a compare-and-swap claim on `paid_paise` against `(net_payable + credit_note_paise) − paid − debited`, plus reversal. `services/purchase_payment_service.py` adds multi-bill allocation and a realized-FX foreign path, reached today only from the bank match queue. `routers/debit_notes.py` (client → vendor, reduces payable) and `routers/purchase_credit_notes.py` (vendor undercharge, increases payable) both CAS-apply to the bill and post through the kernel with rollback. `services/vendor_statement_service.py` builds the ledger and AP ageing off the generated `outstanding_paise` column (migration 278). `services/tds_register_service.py` writes `tds_deductions` at the moment of credit and returns named `statutory_gaps`. `services/itc_reversal_service.py` + `domain/gst/itc_reversal.py` report Rule 37 180-day reversals; `services/itc_register_service.py` classifies posted journals as 4(B)(2)/4(D)(1) and refuses a figure the ledger does not support. `services/treaty_rate_service.py` reads `dtaa_treaty_rates` (migration 310). `routers/document_intelligence_v1.py` extracts an invoice (Groq for PDF text, Gemini for images), stores the original, and refuses to fabricate.

Frontend. `apps/web/app/clients/[id]/purchases/page.tsx` (3143 lines) carries five tabs — Bills, Vendors, Payments, Debit Notes, Credit Notes — reading `purchase_bills`, `vendors`, `purchase_payments`, `debit_notes`, `purchase_credit_notes` directly over PostgREST and writing through the API. `components/purchases/PurchaseBillEditor.tsx` handles create/edit, RCM, multi-currency and AI extraction. Separately `app/accounting/msme-tracker/page.tsx` keeps a manual `msme_payments` table, and `app/accounting/suppliers/page.tsx` maintains a `suppliers` table that nothing in the purchase cycle reads.

Tables: `vendors`, `purchase_bills`, `purchase_bill_lines`, `purchase_payments`, `purchase_payment_allocations`, `debit_notes`, `debit_note_allocations`, `purchase_credit_notes`, `tds_deductions`, `itc_reversal_register`, `dtaa_treaty_rates`, plus the orphans `suppliers`, `msme_vendors`, `msme_payments`.

maturity.rationale: The plumbing is genuinely good — one posting kernel with rollback on every path, integer paise throughout, compare-and-swap on every settlement counter, keyset pagination on every report, a duplicate-bill guard at both the API and the index, and a §195/non-resident engine that is better than anything in the Indian SME market. But three things a CA touches every single day are wrong or absent. (1) The resident TDS thresholds are modelled per-payment when the statute says per-FY-aggregate, so §194J/§194H/§194A silently withhold ZERO on real aggregates, and §194C withholds only on the crossing bill instead of the cumulative — both under-deductions that carry a 30% §40(a)(ia) disallowance, and a test pins the §194C behaviour as correct. (2) §17(5) blocked credit is accepted by the API and used by the GSTR-3B computer but is unreachable from any screen, and the journal debits GST Input for it anyway, so the ledger carries a permanent phantom asset. (3) The GSTR-2A/2B reconciliation — the reason most Indian CAs buy a purchase module at all — asks the CA to export the purchase register the platform already holds to CSV and re-upload it, does the matching in TypeScript, quotes the repealed 105% Rule 36(4) cushion, and writes nothing back. The grade is C rather than D because none of this is architectural: the kernel, the register and the domain modules are the right shapes, and every defect above is a bounded fix inside them.
maturity.would_a_ca_buy_this_module_alone: Not yet — the AP ledger and the foreign-vendor withholding would impress a CA, but a purchase module that under-deducts §194J TDS on aggregates, cannot flag a §17(5) blocked credit, and makes them re-upload their own purchase register to match GSTR-2B is not one they can run a client on.

strengths: The residency-first TDS routing is the best thing in this subsystem and I have seen nothing like it in Tally, Busy or Zoho Books. `domain/tds/residency.py:106-140` transcribes the charging words of each section ('to a resident') rather than inferring, and `routers/purchase_bills.py:530-556` therefore routes a non-resident vendor to §195 as a different CHARGING SECTION — no threshold, rate by nature of income, surcharge and cess — instead of just relabelling the return form. Market tools treat 26Q vs 27Q as a dropdown.

`domain/tds/section_195.py:126-260` asks chargeability BEFORE rate (GE India Technology Centre v. CIT) and REFUSES rather than guessing in exactly three places — no nature recorded, business profits with no no-PE declaration, and a TRC on file with no treaty rate recorded. `services/treaty_rate_service.py:60-111` makes the DTAA position a per-(country, nature) firm fact rather than a per-vendor number. This is the correct posture and it is unusual.

Every purchase-side accounting event goes through the one kernel with a compensating rollback. `routers/purchase_bills.py:1552-1578` flips the bill to received, posts, and rolls the status BACK to draft if `journal_for_purchase_bill` raises — while re-raising a genuine HTTPException so a locked-FY refusal is not collapsed into 'please try again'. `routers/debit_notes.py:500-522` and `services/purchase_payment_service.py:66-116` do the same for their paths.

Lost-update prevention is real, not decorative. `routers/purchase_payments.py:124-175` retries a compare-and-swap on `paid_paise` (`.eq("paid_paise", raw_paid)`) rather than read-check-write, and `routers/debit_notes.py:459-490` does the same on `debited_paise`. `_rollback_bill_claim` (line 177) decrements by its OWN amount rather than restoring a snapshot, so a concurrent payment is not clobbered.

Duplicate supplier invoices are stopped twice and explained once. Migration 313 puts a partial unique index on `(client_id, vendor_id, lower(btrim(bill_no)))` excluding cancelled and soft-deleted rows, and `routers/purchase_bills.py:207-247` re-implements the same predicate purely so the CA gets a sentence naming the existing bill instead of a 23505.

`domain/gst/itc_reversal.py:96-145` gets the two hardest bits of Rule 37 right — proportionate reversal per tax head with CEILING division (documented as deliberate, because under-reversal carries §50 interest and over-reversal is re-availed under Rule 37(4)), and `reversal_period` returning the period IMMEDIATELY FOLLOWING expiry, which is the usual thing to get wrong.

`services/itc_register_service.py:139-158` refuses to register a 4(B)(2) reversal larger than the GST Input credit actually moved on the journal behind it — so a return figure can never exceed what the ledger supports, and the books-vs-ledger comparator stays independent of the register.

Every report in this subsystem obeys the pagination rule. `services/vendor_statement_service.py:37-59`, `services/itc_reversal_service.py:44-70` and `services/itc_register_service.py:50-64` all keyset-walk rather than accepting PostgREST's silent 1000-row truncation, and migration 278's generated `outstanding_paise` column moves the AP-ageing filter into SQL.

Client-assignment scope is enforced on every backend purchase endpoint. `routers/purchase_bills.py:56-100` resolves the owning client from the bill id and returns the SAME 404 for 'not yours' and 'does not exist' so the status code is not an id oracle, and `_assert_batch_scope` (line 96) checks every distinct client in a bulk payload before any row is written.

`services/tds_register_service.py:150-165` records a NIL §195 withholding as a real row with a `non_deduction_reason`, while correctly NOT recording a below-threshold resident bill — 27Q reports non-deduction, 26Q reports deductions, and the docstring says the asymmetry is the statute's.

findings.title: §194J/§194H/§194A/§194D/§194G thresholds are applied per payment when the statute applies them to the FY aggregate — a professional paid ₹30,000 four times has zero TDS deducted
findings.evidence: domain/tds/section_rates.py:104-149 gives every section a `single_threshold_paise` and sets `aggregate_threshold_paise` only on 194C. domain/tds/tds_computer.py:305-310: `applies = taxable_paise > rule.single_threshold_paise or (rule.aggregate_threshold_paise is not None and fy_total > rule.aggregate_threshold_paise)` — for 194J the second clause is dead. I ran it: four ₹30,000 bills under 194J withhold 0 paise against ₹12,000 required; three ₹15,000 bills under 194H withhold 0 against ₹900 required. §194J(1) proviso reads 'if such sum or, as the case may be, the aggregate of the sums credited or paid ... during the financial year does not exceed fifty thousand rupees'; §194H, §194A, §194D and §194G carry the same aggregate wording. The module docstring at section_rates.py:39-45 claims the simplifications 'over-flag rather than silently under-deduct' — for these sections the opposite is true.
findings.ca_experience: A client pays their auditor ₹30,000 a quarter (₹1,20,000 for the year). Every bill posts with tds_paise = 0, nothing reaches tds_deductions, 26Q reports nothing, and the CA discovers it when the assessing officer disallows 30% of ₹1,20,000 under §40(a)(ia) and levies §201(1A) interest at 1%/1.5% a month. Same for rent split across landlords, commission, and interest to non-banks. This is the single most common TDS section a CA firm's SME clients hit.
findings.market_standard: TallyPrime tracks a running FY aggregate per party per nature-of-payment and deducts the moment the exemption limit is crossed; ClearTDS and Winman TDS do the same. No Indian product treats the §194J limit as per-invoice.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `aggregate_threshold_paise` to 194J/194H/194A/194D/194G/193/194 (equal to the single threshold, since the statute states one annual limit), and change the ONE section that genuinely is per-payment — 194I, ₹50,000 per month or part after FA 2025 — to say so in its own comment. `_resolve_bill_resident_tds` already computes `fy_prior` correctly, so only the registry and the `applies` test move.

verification.probe: same probe as TDS-01; s.194H three Rs 15,000 commissions withheld Rs 0 against Rs 900

findings.title: When the §194C ₹1L aggregate is crossed, TDS is deducted only on the crossing bill, not on the cumulative sums — and a test pins the wrong number as correct
findings.evidence: domain/tds/tds_computer.py:313-317 computes `tds = taxable_paise * rate_bps // 10000` — always on THIS bill's taxable only, never on `fy_total`. I ran five ₹25,000 bills to a company contractor: total withheld 50000 paise (₹500) against ₹2,500 required on the ₹1,25,000 aggregate. §194C(5) proviso: 'where the aggregate of the amounts ... credited or paid ... during the financial year exceeds one lakh rupees, the person responsible for paying such sums shall be liable to deduct income-tax under this section' — the liability attaches to the aggregate of such sums, not to the marginal one. tests/test_tds_bill_engine.py:59-70 asserts `b5["tds_paise"] == 500_00`, so the wrong behaviour is locked in by a passing test.
findings.ca_experience: A transporter or job-worker billing ₹25,000 a month: the CA sees ₹500 deducted on the fifth bill and nothing before it. The correct figure is ₹2,500 on the fifth bill (catching up the earlier four). The shortfall disallows 30% of the whole ₹1,25,000 under §40(a)(ia) and attracts §201(1A) interest.
findings.market_standard: TallyPrime's TDS deducts on the cumulative value at the moment the exemption limit is crossed — the standard 'threshold crossed, deduct on aggregate' behaviour every Indian package implements.
findings.suggested_fix: When `applies` is true only because the aggregate clause fired, compute TDS on `fy_total` less TDS already deducted in the FY under that section for that payee, rather than on the current bill alone. The FY-prior figure is already fetched at routers/purchase_bills.py:317-332; it needs a companion sum of prior `tds_paise`. Rewrite tests/test_tds_bill_engine.py:59-70 as the negative control.

verification.probe: ran five Rs 25,000 s.194C bills: Rs 500 total withheld against Rs 2,500 on the aggregate

findings.title: Surcharge and 4% cess are added on top of a DTAA treaty rate, over-deducting on every foreign payment where a treaty applies
findings.evidence: domain/tds/section_195.py:222-256: after the §90(2) branch sets `rate_bps = treaty_rate_bps` and `basis = "treaty"` (lines 218-220), surcharge and cess are applied unconditionally — `sur_pct = _surcharge_percent(...)`, `cess = (base_tax + surcharge) * rates.cess_percent // 100`. I ran a ₹1 crore royalty at a 10% recorded treaty rate: a foreign company withholds 10.40%, a non-corporate payee withholds 11.44% (₹1,44,000 over-deducted). The module explicitly documents and defends its conservative choice for the §206AA floor at lines 244-252 but says nothing about the treaty branch, and tests/test_section_195_rates.py has no test combining a treaty rate with surcharge or cess.
findings.ca_experience: The CA records a Singapore FTS or royalty treaty rate of 10% read off the agreement, and the bill withholds 10.4% or 11.44%. The vendor is short-paid, 27Q reports a rate that does not match the treaty article, and the vendor can only recover the excess by filing an Indian return. On a large remittance this is a conversation with the client's overseas supplier.
findings.market_standard: The settled and mainstream Indian practice — supported by a consistent line of ITAT decisions (e.g. DIC Asia Pacific Pte Ltd v ADIT) — is that a DTAA rate is a ceiling on tax as defined in Article 2, which includes surcharge and cess, so neither is added on top. Winman TDS and ClearTDS cap at the treaty rate.
findings.suggested_fix: When `basis == "treaty"`, do not add surcharge or cess, and say so in the docstring beside the §206AA paragraph that already explains the opposite choice. If the owner wants to keep the conservative behaviour, make it an explicit recorded decision with a test naming it, because right now it is neither documented nor pinned.

verification.what_is_actually_true: A recorded DTAA rate is treated as a base rate and then grossed up by Part II surcharge and 4% cess (domain/tds/section_195.py:256-262), so a 10% treaty rate withholds 10.40% from a foreign company and 11.44% from a non-corporate payee above the surcharge threshold. The settled Indian position (Article 2 'taxes covered' includes surcharge and cess) is that the treaty rate is a ceiling on the total. The module explicitly documents and defends the analogous conservative choice for the s.206AA floor at lines 246-255 but is silent on the treaty branch, and no test pins it either way — so this is neither a recorded decision nor a guarded one.
verification.probe: cd apps/api && python -c "from domain.tds.section_195 import resolve_section_195; ...amount_paise=100_00_00_000 (Rs 1 crore), nature='royalty', trc_on_file=True, form_10f_on_file=True, treaty_rate_bps=1000, fy='2026-27'" printed: company treaty rate_bps 1000 eff_bps 1040 total 104000000 sur 0 cess 4000000 / non-corp treaty rate_bps 1000 eff_bps 1144 total 114400000 sur 10000000 cess 4400000 — i.e. Rs 1,44,000 over-withheld on the non-corporate case.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed, with minor line drift. domain/tds/section_195.py:229-232 sets `rate_bps = treaty_rate_bps; basis = "treaty"` inside the s.90(2) branch; lines 256-262 then run `base_tax = amount_paise * rate_bps // 10000`, `sur_pct = _surcharge_percent(...)` (line 258), `cess = (base_tax + surcharge) * rates.cess_percent // 100` (line 260) unconditionally — there is no `if basis != "treaty"` anywhere between. The module docstring's item 5 (lines 39-45) and the block comment at lines 246-255 justify surcharge+cess generally and specifically defend applying them on top of the s.206AA floor; neither mentions the treaty branch.
lens_notes.guards: None. tests/test_section_195_rates.py has no test combining a non-zero treaty rate with surcharge or cess: test_a_lower_treaty_rate_wins (line 120) asserts only rate_bps and base_tax_paise, never tds_paise; test_a_treaty_rate_of_zero_is_honoured (line 137) asserts tds_paise == 0, which is trivially true at a 0% base. Section 5 of that file (lines 207-260) tests surcharge/cess only on Act-rate paths. No DB constraint, no frontend cap. The one mitigation is presentational: migration 309 stores tds_surcharge_paise / tds_cess_paise separately (routers/purchase_bills.py:547-548), so a CA who looks can see the components — but the withheld total is still wrong.
lens_notes.reach: Live. routers/purchase_bills.py:540 calls _resolve_bill_section_195 on every non-resident bill, which calls resolve_section_195 at line 374; the result becomes tds_paise / net_payable_paise on the bill (lines 542-556). purchase_bills is mounted in main.py. The treaty branch is only entered when trc_on_file is true AND a treaty rate is recorded in dtaa_treaty_rates (migration 310) — i.e. exactly the case a CA has done the work to set up.

findings.title: §17(5) blocked credit is still debited to GST Input in the journal, leaving a permanent phantom asset and a permanent GSTR-3B books-vs-ledger mismatch
findings.evidence: services/phase2_journal_service.py:656-676 debits `gst_input_id` for the FULL `bill["cgst_paise"]`/`sgst_paise`/`igst_paise` with no reference to `ineligible_itc_*_paise`, and the expense debits at lines 640-654 are the taxable amount only. Meanwhile domain/gst/gstr3b_computer.py:663-666 computes `book_igst = sum(p.igst_paise - p.ineligible_igst_paise ...)`, and services/gst_return_service.py:828-830 compares that against the GL `gst_input` movement. Nothing anywhere reverses the ineligible portion out of GST Input.
findings.ca_experience: The client's trial balance carries an Input GST asset that will never be claimed and never clears — a hotel bill, a club membership, a works-contract invoice — while the expense head is understated by the same amount, so profit is overstated. The GSTR-3B books-vs-ledger reconciliation on the same screen reports an unexplained difference every month equal to the blocked GST, and the CA cannot make it agree.
findings.market_standard: TallyPrime posts blocked credit to the expense/purchase ledger at voucher entry (its 'Ineligible for input credit' classification), so the GST Input ledger only ever holds claimable credit. Zoho Books does the same via its ITC-ineligible flag.
findings.suggested_fix: In `journal_for_purchase_bill`, debit GST Input for `cgst_paise - ineligible_itc_cgst_paise` (and the same for SGST/IGST) and add the ineligible remainder to the expense debit — that is what §17(5) means economically. Add a parity test asserting the GL gst_input movement equals `books_itc` for a bill with a blocked line.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The claim is literally correct about the code: services/phase2_journal_service.py:656-676 debits GST Input for the gross tax and nothing subtracts the s.17(5) portion, while services/gst_return_service.py:828-833 compares a books figure that IS net of it — so the moment a blocked line exists there is both a phantom Input GST asset and a permanent books-vs-ledger difference. But no screen can set itc_eligible=false today (see PUR-05), so no real CA has hit this. It is a latent bug that becomes high the instant PUR-05's UI is built, and the two must be fixed together.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed exactly at the cited lines. services/phase2_journal_service.py:656-676 appends three debits to gst_input_id for the full `bill["cgst_paise"]`, `bill["sgst_paise"]`, `bill["igst_paise"]` with no reference to any ineligible field; the expense debits at 645-654 are built from `purchase_bill_lines.taxable_amount_paise` grouped by expense_account_id, so the blocked GST lands nowhere but GST Input. grep for `ineligible_itc` across apps/api returns hits only in routers/purchase_bills.py, services/gst_return_service.py and migration 240 — never in phase2_journal_service.py. The books side does net it: domain/gst/gstr3b_computer.py:663-666 computes `book_igst = sum(p.igst_paise - p.ineligible_igst_paise ...)`, and services/gst_return_service.py:828-830 builds `books_itc` from those and compares it at line 833 against `gl["itc_paise"]`, which (lines 158-167) is the raw Dr-minus-Cr movement on the GST Input account. So the comparator would report a difference equal to the blocked GST.
lens_notes.guards: None on the journal side. No test asserts anything about gst_input and ineligible together (grep over tests/ for gst_input + ineligible/blocked returns nothing), and no migration or trigger reconciles them. The only thing standing between this and a live wrong number is PUR-05.
lens_notes.reach: This is why the severity drops. The bug can only fire on a bill whose lines carry `itc_eligible = false`, and no screen sends that key — apps/web/components/purchases/PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:476-489 builds the line payload with description/hsn_sac/quantity/unit/rate_paise/gst_rate_percent/expense_account_id/service_catalogue_id and nothing else, and no other frontend file writes purchase_bill_lines. So today every bill has ineligible_itc_*_paise = 0, the GST Input debit is correct by accident, and the reconciliation agrees. The defect is latent, not live.

findings.title: §17(5) blocked credit cannot be set from any screen — the API field, the DB column and the return computation all exist and are unreachable
findings.evidence: models/invoices.py:222-246 accepts `itc_eligible` and `blocked_credit_reason` per line; migration 240 adds the columns; routers/purchase_bills.py:466-478 aggregates them; domain/gst/gstr3b_computer.py:668-671 files them in 4(B)(1). A grep for `itc_eligible` and `blocked_credit` across all of apps/web returns ZERO hits, and components/purchases/PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:475-490 builds the line payload with no such key.
findings.ca_experience: GSTR-3B Table 4(B)(1) and 4(D)(1) are permanently nil for every client, so a client with any blocked credit over-claims ITC every month. The only workaround is to leave the GST off the bill entirely, which then misstates the payable to the vendor and breaks the 2B tie-up.
findings.market_standard: TallyPrime asks 'Is ineligible for input credit?' with a §17(5) reason at voucher entry; Zoho Books has a per-line ITC-eligibility dropdown; ClearTax's purchase register carries an ineligibility column. It is a first-class field everywhere.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a per-line 'ITC eligible' toggle plus a §17(5) reason picker to PurchaseBillEditor (the reason codes are listed in migration 240's column comment), and show the blocked total on the bill view drawer. Backend needs no change.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The s.17(5) blocked-credit field is fully implemented in models/invoices.py:245-246, migration 240:29-30, routers/purchase_bills.py:468-478 and domain/gst/gstr3b_computer.py:663-671, and is settable from nowhere — apps/web/components/purchases/PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:476-489 omits it from the save payload and no other frontend file writes bill lines. The one correction to the evidence: the editor DOES carry a §17(5) heuristic warning banner (PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:343,728-739 via lib/purchases/billEditor.ts:144), which flags 'Possible blocked ITC — review before saving' and offers no way to act on it.
verification.probe: grep -rn 'itc_eligible|blocked_credit|itcEligible|blockedCredit' apps/web --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx printed exactly 3 lines, all `blockedCreditHits` (the read-only warning); zero hits for itc_eligible or blocked_credit_reason.

lens_notes.literal: The substance is confirmed; one sentence of the evidence is wrong. Backend and DB exist: models/invoices.py:245-246 declares `itc_eligible: bool = True` and `blocked_credit_reason`, with a validator at 285-286 requiring the reason when eligibility is false; migration 240_purchase_bill_itc_eligibility.sql:29-30 adds both columns with a reason-code list in the COMMENT at line 35; routers/purchase_bills.py:468-478 accumulates `total_ineligible_{cgst,sgst,igst}` and persists them at 764-766; domain/gst/gstr3b_computer.py:663-671 nets them out of book ITC and files them as itc_ineligible_*. The auditor's claim that a grep for itc_eligible/blocked_credit across apps/web 'returns ZERO hits' is FALSE — apps/web/components/purchases/PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:29,343,728-739 has `findBlockedCreditHits` (apps/web/lib/purchases/billEditor.ts:144), a heuristic that renders an amber banner reading 'Possible blocked ITC — review before saving (CGST Act §17(5))'. But that banner is read-only: there is no control that sets itc_eligible, and the save payload at PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:476-489 omits both keys. So the claim that the field cannot be SET stands, and the banner makes it worse — the product warns the CA and then gives them nothing to do about it.
lens_notes.guards: None that close the gap. No other write path exists: grep for `purchase_bill_lines` across apps/web returns nothing (all bill writes go through the API), and grep for `itc_eligible` across apps/api shows only purchase_bills.py, models/invoices.py and tests. tests/test_r239_gst_computation_gaps.py:30-50,186-203 tests the model and the aggregation but is a backend test only — it cannot notice the missing UI.
lens_notes.reach: Per the instructions this CONFIRMS a gap rather than refuting it: the capability exists end-to-end in the backend (accepted, stored, aggregated, filed into GSTR-3B 4(B)/4(D)) and is reachable from no screen. The consequence is live and reaches every client — GSTR-3B Table 4(B)(1)/4(D)(1) is structurally nil, so any client with hotel bills, club memberships, motor vehicles or works-contract inputs over-claims ITC every month.

findings.title: The vendor's TDS rate is collected on a form, shown in a list column, and never used by the computation
findings.evidence: The vendor form at apps/web/app/clients/[id]/purchases/page.tsx:1827 has a 'TDS Rate %' input; line 1216 persists `tds_rate_bps`; line 1378-1379 renders it as a 'Rate' column. On the backend `_resolve_bill_resident_tds` (routers/purchase_bills.py:284-345) never reads `vendor.get("tds_rate_bps")` — it calls `TDSComputer().resolve_tds`, which takes the rate from the FY registry. `grep tds_rate_bps routers/purchase_bills.py` shows only the COMPUTED rate being written back. The one place the constant is even named, `_TDS_DEFAULT_BPS` at routers/purchase_bills.py:30-37 ('Default rates when vendor master tds_rate_bps is 0'), has no readers at all.
findings.ca_experience: A CA with a §197 lower-deduction certificate for 1% types 1 into the vendor's TDS Rate, sees '1.0%' in the vendor list, and every bill deducts 2% or 10%. They only find out when the vendor complains or the certificate limit is reconciled at year end. The UI actively confirms a setting that does nothing.

findings.title: No §197 lower-deduction or nil-deduction certificate anywhere — no certificate number, rate, threshold amount or validity period
findings.evidence: The `vendors` table (migration 049, extended by 201/303/308/309/311) has no certificate column of any kind. `domain/tds/tds_computer.py:38-39` declares `is_lower_deduction` and `lower_deduction_cert` on `TDSDeducteeRecord` and nothing anywhere sets them (grep for `is_lower_deduction` returns only that declaration). `resolve_tds` (line 271) takes no certificate parameter. A grep for `197` across domain/, services/ and routers/ returns only migration/comment noise.
findings.ca_experience: A transport contractor or an advertising agency with a §197 certificate at 0.5% cannot be modelled. The CA must either turn TDS off on the vendor (so no register row, no 26Q deductee line, no challan) or accept over-deduction at the section rate. 26Q's own deductee annexure has a lower-deduction flag and certificate-number field that can never be populated, so the FVU file is wrong for those payees.
findings.market_standard: TallyPrime, ClearTDS, Winman TDS and Saral TDS all hold a §197 certificate per deductee: certificate number, section, rate, the amount up to which it applies, and validity dates, with the rate reverting to the section rate once the certificate limit is exhausted.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `tds_certificate_no`, `tds_certificate_rate_bps`, `tds_certificate_limit_paise`, `tds_certificate_valid_from/to` to vendors; pass them into `resolve_tds` so the certificate rate applies to bills dated in the validity window up to the limit and the section rate applies beyond it; carry the flag and number onto the `tds_deductions` row for 26Q.

verification.what_is_actually_true: There is no s.197 lower/nil-deduction certificate model: `vendors` has no certificate number, rate, limit or validity column (migration 049 and every later vendors ALTER — 201, 303, 308, 309, 311), and `resolve_tds` (domain/tds/tds_computer.py:271) takes no certificate parameter, so a certificate holder is always withheld at the full section rate. The evidence's claim that `is_lower_deduction` exists only as a dataclass field is wrong — it is a real column on tds_deductions (migrations/037_tds_engine.sql:48-49), accepted by routers/tds.py:58-59 and read by apps/web/app/tds/returns/page.tsx:128 — but nothing ever sets it, and the register-driven 26Q builder (services/tds_return_service.py:211-229) omits it entirely, so the FVU lower-deduction fields are permanently False.
verification.probe: grep -A6 'ALTER TABLE public.vendors' apps/api/migrations/{201,303,308,309,311}_*.sql | grep -i 'ADD COLUMN' listed 14 columns, none certificate-related. grep -rn 'is_lower_deduction|lower_deduction' apps/api returned 9 hits across routers/tds.py, migrations/037 and domain/tds/tds_computer.py — none of them a write from the bill path.

lens_notes.literal: The substantive gap is confirmed; two evidence sentences are wrong and need correcting. CONFIRMED: the `vendors` table carries no certificate column of any kind — migration 049 plus every later ALTER (201: credit_days; 303: msme_status, msme_registration_no; 308: residential_status, country_of_residence, tax_identification_number; 309: section_195_nature_of_income, trc_on_file, form_10f_on_file, no_pe_declaration_on_file, treaty_rate_bps; 311: no_pe_declaration_on/_by/_ref) — nothing about s.197. `TDSComputer.resolve_tds` (domain/tds/tds_computer.py:271) takes no certificate parameter, and `_resolve_bill_resident_tds` (routers/purchase_bills.py:284-347) passes none. WRONG in the evidence: (a) grep for `is_lower_deduction` returns more than the declaration — migrations/037_tds_engine.sql:48-49 adds `is_lower_deduction BOOLEAN` and `lower_deduction_cert TEXT` to `tds_deductions`, routers/tds.py:58-59,151-152,201 accepts them on the manual Compute26QRequest deductee list, and apps/web/app/tds/returns/page.tsx:128 reads `is_lower_deduction` off the row when building the 26Q payload. So the deductee-level flag DOES exist end to end. What does not exist is anything that SETS it.
lens_notes.guards: None, and the machinery that exists makes the gap sharper rather than softer. The register-driven 26Q path — services/tds_return_service.py:211-229 — constructs each TDSDeducteeRecord from the bill and vendor and never sets `is_lower_deduction` or `lower_deduction_cert`, so the flag is always False in the generated return. services/tds_register_service.py:150-200 writes the tds_deductions row from the bill and likewise never sets either column. apps/web/app/tds/returns/page.tsx:128 therefore always reads False.
lens_notes.reach: Live. Every resident-TDS bill goes through _resolve_bill_resident_tds and is withheld at the registry section rate with no way to lower it, and the 26Q deductee annexure's lower-deduction fields are structurally unpopulatable from the bill path. The only alternative is turning tds_applicable off on the vendor, which suppresses the tds_deductions row and the 26Q deductee line entirely.

findings.title: A purchase bill can be created and received into a period whose GSTR-3B has already been filed — the filed-return lock that guards sales invoices is missing on both paths
findings.evidence: routers/sales_invoices.py:819-826 calls `period_lock_service.assert_open(...)` on invoice CREATE, right after the FY check. `_create_purchase_bill_core` (routers/purchase_bills.py:757-762) calls only `period_validation_service.validate_posting_date_cached` — no `assert_open`. `receive_purchase_bill` (routers/purchase_bills.py:1533-1536) likewise calls only `validate_posting_date`. The lock IS imported and used in `update_purchase_bill` at lines 1345-1347, so the omission is on create and receive specifically. `services/phase2_journal_service.py` has no `assert_open`/`period_lock_reason` reference, so the kernel does not catch it either. tests/test_documents_locked_by_filed_return.py covers only the purchase-bill EDIT path (line 189).
findings.ca_experience: A late supplier invoice for March arrives in June. The CA books it dated March and receives it. The GSTR-3B for March was filed in April with its own ITC figure. The March books now claim credit the filed return never did, permanently. Nothing warns them, and the books-vs-ledger reconciliation the product prides itself on will disagree for that month forever. The equivalent sales invoice is refused with a sentence naming the filing date.
findings.market_standard: TallyPrime blocks entry into a GST-return-locked period and prompts to move the voucher to the current period; ClearTax's books flag out-of-period ITC. A recipient who genuinely wants that credit takes it in the current 3B under §16(4), which is exactly what the refusal message should say.
findings.suggested_fix: Call `period_lock_service.assert_open(db, firm_id, client_id, bill_date)` in `_create_purchase_bill_core` (mirroring sales_invoices.py:824) and in `receive_purchase_bill` before the status flip. Extend tests/test_documents_locked_by_filed_return.py with a create case and a receive case.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The filed-return period lock is enforced on purchase-bill UPDATE (routers/purchase_bills.py:1345,1347) but not on CREATE (line 740 has only the FY check) or RECEIVE (line 1536, likewise), while the sales side enforces it on create at routers/sales_invoices.py:825. A late bill dated into a period whose GSTR-3B is already filed is accepted and posted, and neither the kernel (no period_lock reference in services/phase2_journal_service.py) nor the test suite (tests/test_documents_locked_by_filed_return.py has only edit cases) notices. Migration 267's own header text names this exact omission as the thing it was written to allow fixing.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed at every cited line. routers/sales_invoices.py:823-826 calls `period_lock_service.assert_open(get_supabase(), firm_id, data.get("client_id"), data.get("invoice_date"))` on invoice CREATE, immediately after `validate_posting_date_cached` at 815-818, with a comment explaining that the FY lock is the CA's switch and this is the portal's. `_create_purchase_bill_core` (routers/purchase_bills.py:737-743) calls only `period_validation_service.validate_posting_date_cached` — the full list of lock calls in that file is lines 740, 1339, 1341, 1345, 1347, 1536, 1699, and `assert_open` appears only at 1345 and 1347 (the UPDATE path). `receive_purchase_bill` at line 1536 calls only `validate_posting_date`, and its own comment ('FY-lock: receiving posts a dated journal') shows it was written with only the FY half in mind.

findings.title: The Rule 37 report ignores debit notes and purchase credit notes, over-reversing ITC on any bill settled by a purchase return
findings.evidence: services/itc_reversal_service.py:57-59 selects only `total_paise, paid_paise, tds_paise, cgst_paise, sgst_paise, igst_paise` — not `debited_paise` or `credit_note_paise`, and not the generated `outstanding_paise` column that migration 278 added precisely to net them. `domain/gst/itc_reversal.py:73-79`: `unpaid = total_paise - (paid + tds)`. Every other AP path in the codebase uses the full formula: routers/purchase_payments.py:150-156, routers/debit_notes.py:471-476 and services/vendor_statement_service.py:305-310 all compute `(net_payable + credit_note_paise) − paid − debited`.
findings.ca_experience: A ₹1,18,000 bill where ₹59,000 of goods were returned on a debit note and the balance was never paid shows as ₹1,18,000 unpaid at 180 days and reverses 100% of the ₹18,000 ITC — but ₹9,000 of that was already reversed by the debit note's own journal. The CA reverses ₹9,000 too much in GSTR-3B Table 4(B)(2), understating credit for the month, and the compensating re-availment is not tracked.
findings.market_standard: ClearTax's and Cygnet's Rule 37 / 180-day reports run off the net outstanding in the purchase ledger, which already reflects debit and credit notes.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `debited_paise, credit_note_paise` to the select and pass them into `reversal_for_bill`, or read `outstanding_paise` directly. The proportion should also be taken against the CURRENT value of the supply, not the original `total_paise`. Add a case to tests/test_rule37_itc_reversal.py with a debit-noted bill as the negative control.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The Rule 37 180-day report computes unpaid as `total_paise - (paid + tds)` (domain/gst/itc_reversal.py:74-77) from a select that omits debited_paise and credit_note_paise (services/itc_reversal_service.py:57-59), so a bill partly settled by a debit note or purchase credit note shows its gross value as unpaid and reverses ITC that the debit note's own journal already credited out of GST Input. The generated `outstanding_paise` column (migration 278:85-93) that every other AP path uses is right there and unread.
verification.probe: cd apps/api && python -c "from domain.gst.itc_reversal import reversal_for_bill; print(reversal_for_bill(total_paise=11800000, paid_paise=0, tds_paise=0, cgst_paise=0, sgst_paise=0, igst_paise=1800000))" printed unpaid_paise 11800000, igst_paise 1800000 (Rs 18,000 reversed). Re-run net of a Rs 59,000 debit note (total 5900000, igst 900000) printed igst_paise 900000 — Rs 9,000, i.e. the report over-reverses by exactly the debit note's ITC.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed. services/itc_reversal_service.py:57-59 selects exactly `id, bill_no, bill_date, vendor_id, status, total_paise, paid_paise, tds_paise, cgst_paise, sgst_paise, igst_paise` — no `debited_paise`, no `credit_note_paise`, no `outstanding_paise`. rule37_report at lines 93-99 passes only total/paid/tds/cgst/sgst/igst into `reversal_for_bill`, and domain/gst/itc_reversal.py:74-77 computes `unpaid = max(0, total_paise - (paid + tds))`. Every other AP path uses the netted formula: routers/purchase_payments.py:153-156 (`effective_payable = net_payable_paise + credit_note_paise; outstanding = effective_payable - paid_paise - debited_paise`), services/vendor_statement_service.py:299,311 (reads the generated `outstanding_paise` column directly). Migration 278:85-93 defines that generated column as net_payable + credit_note - paid - debited, added expressly so the filter could move into the query.
lens_notes.guards: None, and the double-count is real: services/phase2_journal_service.py's journal_for_debit_note (around lines 398-418) credits the GST Input account for the debit note's reversed GST, so the ITC on returned goods has already left the ledger before Rule 37 reverses it a second time. tests/test_rule37_itc_reversal.py and tests/test_rule37_report.py exist but neither exercises a debit-noted or credit-noted bill.

findings.title: No TDS is deducted or recorded on a vendor payment — advances to contractors withhold nothing, and purchase_payments has no tds_paise column at all
findings.evidence: routers/purchase_payments.py:3 and :358 both assert 'TDS already deducted at the purchase bill stage, so payment is net'. `create_purchase_payment` (line 348) and `create_payment_core` (services/purchase_payment_service.py:120) contain no TDS logic — grep for `tds` across both files returns only those two comment lines. `purchase_payments` (migration 050:313, plus 148/159/161/215/226) has no `tds_paise` column, while the AR mirror `receipts` gained one in migration 077:27. `services/tds_register_service.py` is only ever called from `receive_purchase_bill` and `cancel_purchase_bill`. Migration 050:318 explicitly comments that `purchase_bill_id` is nullable 'to support advance payments before bill receipt'.
findings.ca_experience: A client pays a ₹5,00,000 mobilisation advance to a contractor in March; the bill arrives in May. §194C(3) requires deduction at credit OR payment, whichever is EARLIER — so ₹10,000 was due to be deposited by 7 April. The product withholds nothing, creates no tds_deductions row, no challan obligation and no 26Q deductee line for Q4. Interest under §201(1A) runs from the payment date. Advances to vendors are routine in construction, manufacturing and any retainer arrangement.
findings.market_standard: TallyPrime deducts TDS on an advance payment voucher and adjusts it against the bill when the bill is later booked; ClearTDS and Saral both model advance-payment deductions as first-class 26Q rows.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `tds_paise`/`tds_section`/`tds_rate_bps` to purchase_payments; when a payment has no bill allocation (or exceeds the allocated bills), run the same `_resolve_bill_resident_tds` / §195 path over the unallocated amount, post the TDS credit in `journal_for_purchase_payment`, and call `sync_for_bill`'s equivalent for payments so the register carries the row. The adjustment against a later bill needs its own rule so the same sum is not deducted twice.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Nothing on the vendor-payment path deducts or records TDS: purchase_payments has no tds_paise column (migrations/050:312-329; only 215:11 ever alters the table), create_purchase_payment and services/purchase_payment_service.create_payment_core contain no TDS logic, and tds_register_service.sync_for_bill runs only from receive/cancel of a bill (routers/purchase_bills.py:1587,1740). Since §194C(3)/§194J charge at credit or payment whichever is earlier, an unlinked advance — which the UI offers by default for domestic payments at apps/web/app/clients/[id]/purchases/page.tsx:2201 — withholds nothing and creates no deposit obligation, while the AR mirror `receipts` has carried tds_paise since migration 077:27.
verification.probe: grep -in 'tds' apps/api/routers/purchase_payments.py apps/api/services/purchase_payment_service.py printed 2 lines, both docstring comments. grep -rn 'purchase_payments' apps/api/migrations/*.sql | grep -i 'add column' printed 1 line: 215_reversal_support.sql:11 is_reversed.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed at every point. routers/purchase_payments.py:3 ('IT Act Section 194C/194I/194J: TDS already deducted at bill stage; payment is net amount.') and :358 ('TDS was already deducted at the purchase bill stage, so payment is net.') are the ONLY occurrences of 'tds' in either routers/purchase_payments.py or services/purchase_payment_service.py — a case-insensitive grep across both files returns exactly those two lines. `purchase_payments` (migrations/050_sales_purchase_cycle.sql:312-329) has no tds column, and the only later ALTER on that table across all migrations is 215_reversal_support.sql:11 adding `is_reversed`. The AR mirror does have one: migrations/077_collections_ar.sql:27-29 adds `receipts.tds_paise` with a comment naming §194J. Migration 050:311 comments 'purchase_bill_id nullable to support advance payments before bill receipt', and the column at line 316 is indeed nullable.
lens_notes.guards: None. services/tds_register_service.sync_for_bill is called from exactly two places, both bill-lifecycle: routers/purchase_bills.py:1587 (receive) and :1740 (cancel), via the `_sync_tds_register` wrapper at line 1452. There is no payment-side equivalent, so an advance produces no tds_deductions row, no challan obligation, and no 26Q/27Q deductee line.
lens_notes.reach: Live, and the advance path is deliberately exposed in the UI. apps/web/app/clients/[id]/purchases/page.tsx:2201 renders the bill selector with placeholder '— Advance / Select bill —' for domestic payments; line 2205 shows that only FOREIGN payments are forced to link to a bill ('A foreign payment must be linked to the bill it settles — no unlinked foreign advance'). findings.title: The GSTR-2A/2B reconciliation asks the CA to export and re-upload the purchase register the platform already holds, matches in TypeScript, and writes nothing back
findings.evidence: apps/web/app/gst/reconciliation/page.tsx:514 holds `booksRows` in React state populated only from a CSV/XLSX upload (`setBooksRows(rows)` at line 555) — the file never reads `purchase_bills`. The whole matching algorithm is `reconcile()` at lines 225-292, in the browser, keyed on `supplier_gstin|invoice_number` with a 3-paise tolerance. The result is rendered and Excel-exported (line 344) and never persisted. `gstr2a_records` (migration 028) has no `purchase_bill_id` column, so there is no place to store a per-invoice match even if one were computed. This also violates the house rule 'Zero business logic in the frontend'.
findings.ca_experience: The one purchase-side task a CA does every single month — 'which of my client's bills has the supplier not filed, and how much ITC must I hold back' — requires them to export the purchase register from this product, open Excel, download 2B from the portal, upload both back into this product, look at a screen, and then remember the answer, because nothing is written against the bill. Reopening the screen next month starts from zero. There is no supplier-wise defaulter list and no way to see, from the Purchases tab, that a specific bill is unmatched.
findings.market_standard: This is the core of the ITC products CAs actually pay for. ClearTax GST, Cygnet, IRIS Sapphire and TaxGenie all pull 2A/2B, match invoice-by-invoice against the books with fuzzy invoice-number handling, persist a status per invoice, and produce a supplier-wise 'not filed' follow-up list. TallyPrime 5.0 downloads GSTR-2B and reconciles inside the ledger.
findings.suggested_fix: Move `reconcile()` to a backend service that reads `purchase_bills` for the period, add `gstr2a_records.purchase_bill_id` plus a match status, persist the result, and surface the status as a column on the Purchases → Bills tab and as a supplier-wise defaulter list. Keep the CSV upload for the 2B side only.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The purchase register is never read from the platform's own data on either reconciliation path: /gst/reconciliation/page.tsx:514,555 takes it from a CSV upload and matches in the browser (:225-292) with no persistence, and the server-side alternative at routers/gst_workspace.py:830-905 requires the CA to paste a `book_invoices` array (:852) — it persists only a result blob on gstr2b_uploads, not a per-invoice status, and gstr2a_records (migration 028:2-17) has no purchase_bill_id to hold one.

findings.title: The reconciliation screen tells the CA that ITC is restricted to 105% of GSTR-2A — a cushion repealed on 1 January 2022 — while the backend correctly uses 100%

findings.title: §194Q deducts 0.1% on the whole purchase value instead of on the value exceeding ₹50 lakh, and has no FY aggregate at all
findings.evidence: domain/tds/section_rates.py:141: `"194Q": TDSSectionRule(50_00_000_00, 10, 10)` — a single threshold with `aggregate_threshold_paise=None`. domain/tds/tds_computer.py:315 then computes `tds = taxable_paise * rate_bps // 10000` on the full amount. I ran a single ₹60,00,000 bill: 600000 paise (₹6,000) withheld, against the statutory ₹1,000 (0.1% of the ₹10,00,000 exceeding ₹50L). And because there is no aggregate, one hundred ₹1,00,000 bills totalling ₹1 crore from the same seller withhold nothing at all. §194Q(1) charges 0.1% 'of such sum exceeding fifty lakh rupees' where the value 'or aggregate of such value' in the year exceeds ₹50 lakh.
findings.ca_experience: Two opposite wrong numbers for the same client. A trading SME buying in many small lots crosses ₹50 lakh with a supplier and deducts nothing all year — §40(a)(ia) disallowance on the excess. A client with one large bill deducts six times what is due and the supplier is short-paid. §194Q applies to any buyer with turnover above ₹10 crore, which is most of the SMEs a CA firm serves.
findings.market_standard: TallyPrime tracks 194Q per party cumulatively and deducts on the incremental value above ₹50 lakh, and also handles the §194Q vs §206C(1H) precedence (if the buyer deducts under 194Q, the seller does not collect under 206C(1H)).
findings.suggested_fix: Give 194Q an excess-only computation: `tds = max(0, fy_total - 50L) * rate - tds_already_deducted_in_fy`, with the aggregate as the trigger. Note that §206C(1H) TCS is separately unimplemented — section_rates.py:143-149 says so explicitly for 206C — so the precedence rule cannot be modelled until TCS exists.

verification.what_is_actually_true: §194Q is computed as 0.1% of the whole bill once a single bill exceeds ₹50 lakh, and not at all otherwise: a ₹60,00,000 bill withholds ₹6,000 against the statutory ₹1,000 (§194Q(1) charges 0.1% of 'such sum exceeding fifty lakh rupees'), and one hundred ₹1,00,000 bills totalling ₹1 crore withhold nil because section_rates.py:141 sets no aggregate threshold. Borderline critical — a wrong tax figure is deducted, paid and reported.
verification.probe: cd apps/api && venv/bin/python -c "from domain.tds.tds_computer import TDSComputer; ..." printed: single 60L bill -> TDSResolution(applies=True, section='194Q', tds_paise=600000, rate_pct=0.1, ...) i.e. ₹6,000; 100 x ₹1L bills -> total tds paise 0 on an FY total of ₹1,00,00,000.

findings.title: The MSME §43B(h) tracker is a manually re-keyed side table with the whole statutory rule computed in TypeScript, disconnected from purchase bills and from vendors.msme_status
findings.evidence: apps/web/app/accounting/msme-tracker/page.tsx:59-88 implements the entire §43B(h) test in the browser — `due_days = agreement_type === "written" ? 45 : 15`, `addDays`, and a `status`/`disallowed_paise` decision — and reads/writes `msme_payments` directly over PostgREST (lines 156, 263). It never touches `purchase_bills`, `vendors` or `purchase_payments`. Separately, `vendors.msme_status` (migration 303:186) IS modelled, feeds `public.schedule_iii_ageing`, and is settable only from the Schedule III ageing report (app/clients/[id]/reports/ageing/page.tsx:441). There is no backend §43B(h) code at all — grep for `43B` across apps/api returns only migration comments. There is also no MSMED §16 interest computation anywhere. A third dead table, `msme_vendors` (migration 014:393), has zero readers.
findings.ca_experience: Every MSME supplier invoice must be typed in a second time by hand, with the amount, date and agreement type re-entered, and it does not reconcile to the bills already in the system. The disallowance figure is computed in the browser and is not available to the income-tax computation. Vendors classified micro/small for the Schedule III note are invisible to the tracker and vice versa. No interest under MSMED §16 (three times the RBI bank rate, compounded monthly) is computed, and §43B(h) is stricter than the code models: MSMED §15 caps the agreed period at 45 days but the agreed period may be SHORTER, so a written agreement saying 30 days is treated as 45 here and a genuine disallowance is missed.
findings.market_standard: TallyPrime 4.1+ ships MSME tracking off the actual party ledger with an ageing report against the §15 due date; Zoho Books flags MSME vendors on the bill; ClearTax's 43B(h) report is generated from the purchase register, not re-keyed.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete the manual table and derive §43B(h) on the backend from `purchase_bills` + `purchase_payments` for vendors whose `msme_status` is micro or small, with the agreed credit period read from `purchase_bills.credit_days` (already snapshotted) capped at 45 days, defaulting to 15 where no agreement is recorded. Report the year-of-accrual disallowance and the §16 interest, and surface the vendor's MSME classification on the vendor master where the CA already is.

findings.title: Import of goods has no path — no Bill of Entry, so the IGST paid to customs cannot be recorded and GSTR-3B 4(A)(1)/(2) are hard-coded nil
findings.evidence: A grep for `bill of entry`, `bill_of_entry`, `BoE` and `import of goods` across apps/api finds nothing but a comment in migration 309 and a `customs` value in the exchange-rate-type enum (domain/currency/rate_types.py:12). domain/gst/gstr3b_computer.py:293-299 emits `("IMPG", 0, 0, 0, 0)` and `("IMPS", 0, 0, 0, 0)` unconditionally, with the docstring at line 280 conceding 'nothing upstream distinguishes an import ... from any other purchase yet'.
findings.ca_experience: For an importing client the IGST paid on the Bill of Entry — often the largest single ITC item of the month — cannot be booked at all. Putting it on the vendor's bill overstates Trade Payables by the IGST (the supplier was never charged it); leaving it off loses the credit. GSTR-3B Table 4(A)(1) files nil against a 2B that shows the BoE, and the CA must file outside the product.

Import of services is the §195/RCM combination that already half-exists and needs the `IMPS` row wired.

findings.title: Reverse-charge bills produce no self-invoice (§31(3)(f)) and no payment voucher (§31(3)(g))
findings.evidence: `is_reverse_charge` is accepted (models/invoices.py:309), drives the payable exclusion (routers/purchase_bills.py:499-505) and the self-assessed output credit in the journal (services/phase2_journal_service.py:705-718). findings.ca_experience: Where the RCM supply comes from an unregistered supplier, §31(3)(f) requires the recipient to issue a self-invoice — within 30 days of receipt since Rule 47A (01-11-2024) — and §31(3)(g) requires a payment voucher. Neither exists, so the client has an RCM liability discharged in 3B with no invoice behind it. In a departmental audit the ITC on that RCM is challenged for want of the document Rule 36(1)(b) requires.

findings.title: GST compensation cess cannot be recorded on a purchase, so the cess ITC is lost for every client dealing in cess goods
findings.evidence: `purchase_bills` has `ineligible_itc_cess_paise` (migration 240:41) but no `cess_paise` column at all — grep of the migrations confirms it. `purchase_bill_lines` has no cess rate or amount. services/gst_return_service.py:684 reads `int(b.get("cess_paise") or 0)` on a purchase bill, which is therefore always 0, and domain/gst/gstr3b_computer.py:690 sets `result.itc_cess = book_cess` from that. `_compute_line_gst` (routers/purchase_bills.py:133-155) computes only CGST/SGST/IGST.
findings.ca_experience: A client buying aerated drinks, tobacco, coal, or motor vehicles pays compensation cess on every inward invoice and it can be recorded nowhere. GSTR-3B Table 4(A) cess is nil, the credit is never claimed, and the trade payable to the vendor is understated by the cess, so the vendor ledger will not agree with the supplier's statement.
findings.market_standard: Cess is a standard rate field on the purchase line in TallyPrime, Busy, Marg and Zoho Books India, and flows to 3B Table 4 cess automatically.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `cess_rate_bps` and `cess_paise` to purchase_bill_lines and `cess_paise` to purchase_bills, compute it alongside the other heads in `_compute_line_gst`, include it in the payable and the journal, and expose a cess column on the bill editor. The GST computer and the ineligible-cess column are already waiting for it.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Compensation cess cannot be recorded on a purchase anywhere: purchase_bills and purchase_bill_lines have no cess column (production schema fixture), so the GSTR-3B ITC cess line is structurally always nil and the vendor payable is understated by the cess on any cess-bearing bill. The same hole exists on the SALES side (client_sales_invoices / client_sales_invoice_lines also have no cess column — the gstr1_builder.py:634-640 comment already flags this as latent), so this is a product-wide absence of compensation cess, not a purchase-only one. Medium is defensible but it borders on high: the trade payable to the vendor is a wrong money figure, not merely a missing disclosure.
verification.probe: python -c "json.load(open('tests/fixtures/production_schema_2026-09-03.json'))" -> purchase_bills cess cols: ['ineligible_itc_cess_paise', 'tds_cess_paise']; purchase_bill_lines cess cols: []; client_sales_invoice_lines cess: []; client_sales_invoices cess: [].

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed, and the production schema settles it. purchase_bills has exactly two cess columns — `ineligible_itc_cess_paise` (migration 240:41) and `tds_cess_paise` (migration 309:117, the §195 health-and-education cess, unrelated to compensation cess) — and NO `cess_paise`. purchase_bill_lines has no cess column at all. So services/gst_return_service.py:684 `cess_paise=int(b.get('cess_paise') or 0)` is unconditionally 0, and domain/gst/gstr3b_computer.py:690 `result.itc_cess = book_cess` therefore always reports nil ITC cess. routers/purchase_bills.py:137-160 `_compute_line_gst` returns a 3-tuple (cgst, sgst, igst) with no cess term.
lens_notes.guards: None that record cess. firm_hsn_rate_history carries `cess_rate_pct` / `cess_specific_paise_per_unit` (migration 181:31-32) but the only code that touches them is the Pydantic model models/firm_hsn_rate_history.py:17-33 — no computation reads them, and migration 181:17 says so explicitly ('No automatic slab/cess/RCM branching logic'). No frontend cess field exists in apps/web/components/purchases/*.

findings.title: AI-extracted invoice figures are never arithmetically validated and are never reconciled against what the CA saves
findings.evidence: routers/document_intelligence_v1.py:204-234 (`_parse_extraction_json`) coerces the paise fields to int and returns them with no check that `taxable + cgst + sgst + igst == total`, and no check that the line items sum to the header. `_estimate_confidence` (line 268) counts populated fields only — it is field presence, not accuracy. On the frontend, components/purchases/PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:441-455 uses ONLY `ex.line_items` to build the editor lines and discards the extracted `total_paise`/`taxable_amount_paise` entirely, so nothing tells the CA whether the lines they are about to save add up to the invoice total the model read.
findings.ca_experience: A model that misreads one digit of one line, or drops a line entirely from a multi-page invoice, produces a bill that looks plausible and is short. Nothing on the screen compares the reconstructed total against the invoice total, and 'confidence: high' is displayed for an extraction whose arithmetic does not close. If the model returns a total but no line items, the CA gets an empty bill with a filled header.
findings.market_standard: Dext, Zoho Books Autoscan and Vyapar all show the original document side by side with the extracted fields and flag when the line total does not equal the header total before allowing a save.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate the arithmetic server-side in `_parse_extraction_json` and return an explicit `arithmetic_ok` flag plus the extracted total; in the editor, show the extracted invoice total against the running line total and block the save (or warn hard) when they differ. Also show the stored `document_url` beside the form so the CA can check against the original.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Extraction arithmetic is never validated server-side (routers/document_intelligence_v1.py:216-240) and the extracted header totals are discarded by the editor, which rebuilds the bill from `ex.line_items` only (apps/web/components/purchases/PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:441-455) — so nothing compares the reconstructed total against the invoice total the model read, and there is no side-by-side view of the original (the editor only prints '📎 Original invoice attached', PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:647-650). The finding's 'confidence: high is displayed' and 'empty bill with a filled header' details are refuted: confidence is computed (line 275) but never rendered anywhere in apps/web, and the editor's validation blocks a lineless save.
verification.probe: grep -rn 'confidence' apps/web/app apps/web/components apps/web/lib --include='*.tsx' --include='*.ts' -> no hit in the purchases tree (only relationships/, memory/, banking/, HsnLookup). grep -rn 'from-document' apps/web -> no callers.

lens_notes.literal: The core claim is confirmed; two supporting details in the finding are wrong. Confirmed: `_parse_extraction_json` (routers/document_intelligence_v1.py:216-240) coerces the five paise fields and the per-line fields to numbers and returns — no check that taxable+cgst+sgst+igst == total, none that the lines sum to the header. `_estimate_confidence` (line 275-294) scores field PRESENCE only (vendor_name, vendor_gstin, invoice_no, invoice_date, total_paise>0, 2 points each). apps/web/components/purchases/PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:441-455 builds editor lines from `ex.line_items` alone and never reads `ex.total_paise` / `ex.taxable_amount_paise`. WRONG in the finding: (a) the confidence label is never rendered — grep for 'confidence' across apps/web returns no hit in the purchases tree, and the editor shows only the static banner '✓ AI extracted data pre-filled below. Review before saving.' (PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:642-646); (b) 'a total but no line items gives an empty bill with a filled header' does not happen on this path — validateBillEditor requires at least one valid line (PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:330, :468-469; lib/purchases/billEditor.test.ts:42-51), so the save is blocked. That scenario belongs to POST /purchase-bills/from-document (routers/purchase_bills.py:1853-1855, which writes header totals straight from the extraction and inserts lines only `if line_items`), and NOTHING in apps/web calls /from-document.
lens_notes.guards: Partial only. The saved bill's totals are always recomputed from the lines by `_compute_bill_lines_and_totals` (routers/purchase_bills.py:414+), so the bill is internally consistent — but that is exactly what hides the problem: a dropped or mis-read line produces a self-consistent bill that is simply short. The bill is always created as a draft needing a human /receive (routers/purchase_bills.py:1776-1780), which is a review gate but not an arithmetic check. No test asserts extraction arithmetic.
lens_notes.reach: Reachable. POST /api/document-intelligence-v1/extract-invoice is called from PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:416 and the router is mounted at apps/api/main.py:320. The /from-document endpoint is mounted but has no frontend caller.

findings.title: One payment settling several bills is not reachable from the Purchases screen — the multi-bill allocation engine exists but only the bank match queue can use it
findings.evidence: `services/purchase_payment_service.create_payment_core` implements full multi-bill allocation with `unallocated_paise` and per-bill CAS (lines 120-330). Its only caller is `services/bank_posting_service.py:1044`. The Payments tab posts to `POST /api/purchase-payments` (apps/web/app/clients/[id]/purchases/page.tsx:2033) and `components/purchases/PurchaseBillViewDrawer.tsx:465` does too — both hit `routers/purchase_payments.create_purchase_payment`, which takes a single optional `purchase_bill_id` (line 373). The form (page.tsx:1907-1912) has one `billId` state.
findings.ca_experience: A client makes one NEFT of ₹4,50,000 settling six supplier bills. The CA either records six payments with six fabricated references and six journal entries against one bank line, or records one unallocated payment which then sits as an advance and leaves all six bills showing as outstanding in the AP ageing.
findings.market_standard: In TallyPrime a payment voucher shows the party's pending bills for Agst Ref selection; Zoho Books' vendor payment lets you tick multiple bills and shows the unapplied remainder as an advance. This is table stakes.
findings.suggested_fix: Point the Payments tab's form at the multi-bill engine — list the vendor's open bills with allocation boxes, an auto-apply-oldest-first button and a visible unallocated remainder. The backend is done; this is UI plus an endpoint that reaches `create_payment_core`.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The multi-bill allocation engine (services/purchase_payment_service.py:120-330) and a re-allocation endpoint (routers/purchase_payments.py:528) both exist and are reachable from no screen — apps/web calls neither ('/allocate' has zero frontend hits); the Payments tab and the bill drawer both post a single optional purchase_bill_id. A one-NEFT-many-bills settlement can only be done by the bank match queue (services/bank_posting_service.py:1044) or by six separate payments. Additionally, a bill-less payment recorded from the UI leaves unallocated_paise at the DEFAULT 0 (routers/purchase_payments.py:466-481 vs migration 226:36), so even the advance amount is not recorded as unallocated.
verification.probe: grep -rn '/allocate' apps/web --include='*.ts' --include='*.tsx' -> no output. grep -rn 'create_payment_core' apps/api --include='*.py' -> only services/bank_posting_service.py:1044 outside the service and tests.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed. `create_payment_core` (services/purchase_payment_service.py:120-330) takes `data['allocations']`, validates sum(allocated) <= amount, sets `unallocated_paise = amount - total_allocated`, pre-validates every allocation against live outstanding and CAS-updates each bill. Its only non-test caller is services/bank_posting_service.py:1044. routers/purchase_payments.create_purchase_payment (line 348-526) is a separate single-bill implementation taking one optional `purchase_bill_id` (:374) and never touching allocations. The Payments tab posts a single `purchase_bill_id` (apps/web/app/clients/[id]/purchases/page.tsx:2043) from one `billId` state (:1909), as does PurchaseBillViewDrawer.tsx:465.
lens_notes.guards: There IS a second backend door the finding missed: PATCH /api/purchase-payments/{payment_id}/allocate (routers/purchase_payments.py:528-559 -> purchase_payment_service.update_allocations_core), written precisely to resolve a stranded advance across bills. It does not rescue the CA, because grep for '/allocate' across all of apps/web returns ZERO hits — neither the AP nor the AR allocation endpoint is called from any screen. Per the instructions, a backend capability reachable from no screen CONFIRMS the gap.
lens_notes.reach: The single-bill path is the one users get. Worse for the workaround the finding describes: the router's own single-bill insert (routers/purchase_payments.py:466-481) never writes `unallocated_paise` at all, so a UI payment recorded with no bill leaves the column at its DEFAULT 0 (migration 226:36) — the advance is not even flagged as unallocated.

findings.title: Issuing a debit note (purchase return) does not resync the TDS register, so 26Q keeps reporting the pre-return payment amount
findings.evidence: routers/debit_notes.py:418-560 (`issue_debit_note`) applies the note to the bill's `debited_paise`, posts the journal and updates the note — it never calls `_sync_tds_register` or `services.tds_register_service.sync_for_bill`. The same is true of `issue_purchase_credit_note` (routers/purchase_credit_notes.py:419-565), which INCREASES the payable. The register row written at receive time carries `payment_amount_paise = bill.taxable_amount_paise` (services/tds_register_service.py:200) and is never revisited.
findings.ca_experience: A ₹2,00,000 contractor bill has ₹80,000 returned on a debit note. The 26Q deductee row still says ₹2,00,000 was credited to that PAN, and the TDS shown is on the full amount. The vendor's 26AS shows income they did not receive, and the reconciliation between the TDS register and the purchase ledger will not close at year end.
findings.market_standard: TallyPrime adjusts the TDS on a purchase return against the party's deduction so the 26Q figures track the net credit.
findings.suggested_fix: Call `sync_for_bill` after a debit note or purchase credit note is issued against a bill, with the bill's post-note taxable amount. Note this also raises a genuine statutory question the owner should decide: whether the TDS itself is adjusted or only the reported gross.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Issuing a debit note or a purchase credit note against a received bill never resyncs tds_deductions — the only two callers of sync_for_bill are receive (routers/purchase_bills.py:1587) and cancel (:1740) — so the register keeps `payment_amount_paise` = the bill's original taxable amount (services/tds_register_service.py:229). This also contradicts the module's own stated design, which says sync_for_bill 'is called on every transition rather than only on create' (services/tds_register_service.py:21-23). Medium, not high: whether a purchase return should reduce the amount already CREDITED under §194C(3) is a genuine statutory choice the finding itself flags, so the wrongness is in the register never being revisited, not in a settled number being miscomputed.
verification.probe: grep -rn 'sync_for_bill|_sync_tds_register' apps/api --include='*.py' -> outside services/tds_register_service.py and tests, only routers/purchase_bills.py:1469, :1587, :1740. grep -n 'tds' apps/api/routers/debit_notes.py apps/api/routers/purchase_credit_notes.py -> no hits.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed. `_sync_tds_register` / `sync_for_bill` has exactly two call sites in the whole codebase: routers/purchase_bills.py:1587 (inside receive_purchase_bill) and :1740 (inside cancel_purchase_bill). routers/debit_notes.py:419-520 (`issue_debit_note`) only CAS-updates `debited_paise` and the bill status (:484-486) and posts the journal; grep for 'tds' in that file returns nothing. routers/purchase_credit_notes.py:420-520 (`issue_purchase_credit_note`) is the same for `credit_note_paise`. The register row's `payment_amount_paise` is written as `int(bill.get('taxable_amount_paise') or 0)` (services/tds_register_service.py:229) and the bill's taxable_amount_paise is not changed by a note, so the row keeps the pre-return figure.
lens_notes.guards: None. No DB trigger, no scheduled sweep (nothing under apps/api/jobs mentions tds), no reconciliation report. The cancel path DOES resync (routers/purchase_bills.py:1737-1741, with the comment 'The credit is undone, so the deduction never happened'), and cancellation is blocked outright when notes exist (routers/purchase_bills.py:1683), which means the debit-note route is the one path that changes the credited amount and leaves the register stale. PATCH /purchase-bills/{id} does not resync either, but `_reject_locked_bill_fields` (:1215) freezes the amount fields once received, so that one is moot.
lens_notes.reach: Reachable — debit notes and purchase credit notes are first-class UI objects (apps/web/components/purchases/DebitNoteEditor.tsx, PurchaseCreditNoteEditor.tsx) and both routers are mounted.

findings.title: AP ageing lists only bills, so unallocated vendor advances are invisible and the ageing total does not equal the vendor ledger balance
findings.evidence: `VendorStatementService.ap_aging` (services/vendor_statement_service.py:287-346) reads only `purchase_bills` with `outstanding_paise > 0`; `purchase_payments.unallocated_paise` (migration 226:36) is never read there, and no negative/advance row is emitted. `build_statement` (line 71) DOES include every payment, so the vendor statement's closing balance and the AP ageing total legitimately differ whenever an advance exists.
findings.ca_experience: A ₹3,00,000 advance to a supplier makes the vendor statement show a ₹3,00,000 debit while the AP ageing shows the full gross bills with nothing netted. The CA cannot tie the ageing report to the Trade Payables control account, which is exactly the tie-up the Schedule III payables note needs.
findings.market_standard: Tally's Bills Payable report shows 'On Account' amounts as a separate line; Zoho Books shows unapplied vendor advances in the payables ageing summary.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an 'advances / on account' section to `ap_aging` sourced from `purchase_payments.unallocated_paise` (net of reversed payments) and report the reconciling total, so the ageing agrees with the AP control account.

verification.what_is_actually_true: AP ageing reads only purchase_bills with outstanding_paise > 0 (services/vendor_statement_service.py:293-300); vendor advances appear nowhere in it, while the vendor statement debits every payment (services/vendor_statement_service.py:118-125) and the GL debits Trade Payables for the full payment (services/phase2_journal_service.py:771-777) — so the ageing total cannot be tied to the control account whenever an advance exists. One correction to the suggested fix: sourcing it from `purchase_payments.unallocated_paise` alone would still miss UI-created advances, because the single-payment router path never writes that column (routers/purchase_payments.py:466-481 vs its DEFAULT 0 in migration 226:36); the advance has to be derived from amount_paise minus allocations. Note also that a supplier advance is an asset, so excluding it from the Schedule III trade-payables note is correct — the defect is the operational tie-up, not the statutory disclosure.
verification.probe: grep -n 'unallocated' apps/api/services/vendor_statement_service.py -> no output (vs. 4 hits in customer_statement_service.py, where ar_relief_paise at :295 does add receipts.unallocated_paise).

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed. `ap_aging` (services/vendor_statement_service.py:286-350) selects from `purchase_bills` only, filtered `.gt('outstanding_paise', 0)` (:300), and emits `buckets` + `bills` + `total_outstanding_paise`. It never queries purchase_payments and emits no advance/on-account row. `generate` (:246-249) DOES fetch every non-reversed purchase_payment and `build_statement` (:118-125) posts each as a debit against the vendor, so the statement's closing balance nets advances and the ageing total does not.
lens_notes.guards: None. The GL confirms the mismatch rather than bounding it: `journal_for_purchase_payment` (services/phase2_journal_service.py:749-798) debits Trade Payables for the FULL amount_paise regardless of allocation, so an unapplied advance reduces the Trade Payables control balance while leaving every bill's outstanding_paise untouched — the ageing total and the control account genuinely diverge.
lens_notes.reach: Reachable. GET /api/vendors/ap-aging (routers/vendors.py:823-849) -> apps/web/lib/api/index.ts:2068 -> apps/web/app/clients/[id]/reports/ageing/page.tsx:205 (`api.ageing.payables`). The Schedule III note beside it is a separate SQL function, so the Schedule III disclosure itself is unaffected.

findings.title: No purchase orders, goods receipt notes or three-way matching
findings.evidence: A grep for `purchase_order`, `purchase order`, `goods receipt` and `grn` across all of apps/api and apps/web returns nothing. `purchase_bills` has no PO reference column and the bill editor has no PO lookup.
findings.ca_experience: For a trading or manufacturing client the CA cannot answer 'was this bill authorised, and did the goods actually arrive at the quantity billed'. Every bill is entered on trust. It also blocks the commitment/open-PO figure a year-end review would want.
findings.market_standard: TallyPrime, Busy and Marg all ship Purchase Order → Receipt Note → Purchase Bill with quantity and rate matching; Zoho Books has PO → Bill conversion with a match indicator. For an SME's own staff using the platform this is a standard expectation.
findings.suggested_fix: If the target user is the CA rather than the client's purchase clerk, this may be deliberately out of scope — it is worth an explicit owner decision rather than a build. If built, a lightweight PO with a bill-conversion path and a quantity-variance flag covers most of the value.

verification.what_is_actually_true: No purchase order, goods receipt note, or three-way match exists anywhere in the repo — one grep hit, and it is an unrelated comment in a test. Because inventory IS built and stock-in happens at bill receipt (routers/purchase_bills.py:1750 via domain/inventory_service), a trading or manufacturing client's stock moves with nothing evidencing that the goods arrived at the quantity billed. Medium is right, and the finding's own caveat is the right one: this is an owner scope decision (CA-facing vs. client's purchase clerk), not an obvious build.

findings.title: No recurring purchase bills, though recurring sales invoices are fully built
findings.evidence: migration 107 creates `recurring_invoice_templates`, `recurring_invoice_template_lines` and `recurring_invoice_runs`; `services/recurring_invoice_service.py` and `routers/recurring_invoices.py` drive them. Grepping both files for `purchase` returns nothing, and there is no equivalent table or service for purchase bills.
findings.ca_experience: Monthly rent (§194I), a retainer to a consultant (§194J), electricity and telecom bills, and software subscriptions all have to be keyed by hand every month for every client. These are exactly the bills where TDS applies and where a missed month causes a threshold and a challan to be missed too.
findings.market_standard: Zoho Books has recurring bills; TallyPrime has voucher templates and repeat entry; Busy has recurring vouchers.
findings.suggested_fix: Mirror the recurring-invoice tables and service for purchase bills, creating DRAFTS (never auto-receiving, per the house rule) so a human still posts them.

verification.what_is_actually_true: There is no recurring purchase bill: migration 107 and services/recurring_invoice_service.py are sales-only, and no purchase equivalent exists. The finding's 'keyed by hand every month' overstates it slightly — the editor supports Duplicate (apps/web/components/purchases/PurchaseBillEditor.tsx:174-189) and there is a bulk endpoint (routers/purchase_bills.py:904) — but nothing is scheduled and nothing flags a month that was missed, which is the real exposure for §194I/§194J bills.
