findings.title: Vendor payment numbering is count+1, so a deleted or compensated payment guarantees a collision the CA has to retry by hand
findings.evidence: `_next_payment_seq` (routers/purchase_payments.py:218-230 and the identical copy at services/purchase_payment_service.py:52-64) returns `(resp.count or 0) + 1` over rows matching `VPMT-{fy}-%`. Migration 159:143 puts `UNIQUE (firm_id, payment_no)` on the table, and `_compensate_failed_settlement` (services/purchase_payment_service.py:105) DELETEs the payment row on a settlement failure. `_is_unique_violation` then surfaces a 409 'A payment numbering collision was detected; please retry.'
findings.ca_experience: After any failed-and-compensated payment, the next payment attempt collides and the CA sees a 409 they must click through. Two CAs recording payments at the same moment hit it too. It is recoverable but it is a self-inflicted error the CA has to understand.
findings.market_standard: Tally and Zoho use a monotonic sequence that never reuses a number, so a voided voucher leaves a gap rather than causing a collision.
findings.suggested_fix: Take the max existing suffix rather than the count, or move numbering into services/numbering.py with a DB sequence, as the sales side's document numbering already contemplates.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Numbering is count+1 rather than max+1 (apps/api/routers/purchase_payments.py:218-230; apps/api/services/purchase_payment_service.py:44-55) against a UNIQUE (firm_id, payment_no) constraint (migration 159:144-145), which is fragile. But the finding's premise is wrong: the only delete path (services/purchase_payment_service.py:105) removes the just-created, highest-numbered row, so a compensated payment does NOT guarantee a later collision. The reachable cases are concurrent creation, and the `except -> return 1` fallback that hands out VPMT-{fy}-0001 whenever the count query throws. Severity stays low — a 409 the CA retries, with the journal already compensated.
verification.probe: `grep -n '@router.delete|def delete' apps/api/routers/purchase_payments.py` -> no matches; `grep 'purchase_payments").*delete' apps/api/routers/purchase_payments.py apps/api/services/purchase_payment_service.py` -> one hit, services/purchase_payment_service.py:105.

lens_notes.literal: The mechanism is literal, the harm is not. `_next_payment_seq` really is `(resp.count or 0) + 1` over `like('payment_no', f'VPMT-{fy}-%')` in both copies (apps/api/routers/purchase_payments.py:218-230, apps/api/services/purchase_payment_service.py:44-55), migration 159:144-145 really does add UNIQUE (firm_id, payment_no), and the 409 'A payment numbering collision was detected; please retry.' exists at routers/purchase_payments.py:116-120 and services/purchase_payment_service.py:325,546-549. But the stated trigger is wrong: `_compensate_failed_settlement` (services/purchase_payment_service.py:105) deletes the payment it just created, which is the HIGHEST-numbered row, so the count returns to N and the next attempt legitimately gets N+1 again — no collision. A collision needs a hole BELOW the top.
lens_notes.guards: No user-facing delete endpoint exists (`grep '@router.delete' apps/api/routers/purchase_payments.py` -> nothing) and the compensation delete at services/purchase_payment_service.py:105 is the only DELETE against the table, so ordinary use never punches a mid-sequence hole. There is no retry loop around the insert — the 409 is surfaced straight to the caller — and the journal is compensated first (routers/purchase_payments.py:63-118), so a collision does not leave a phantom GL entry.
lens_notes.reach: Two paths do reach a CA. (1) Genuine concurrency: two payments computed against the same count both build VPMT-{fy}-{N}; the loser gets the 409. (2) The `except: return 1` fallback at routers/purchase_payments.py:228-229 and services/purchase_payment_service.py:54-55 — any transient failure of the count query hands out VPMT-{fy}-0001, which collides for every firm that already has one payment this FY, and retrying does not fix it while the count query stays broken.

findings.title: Duplicate-bill detection is exact-match on vendor plus bill number only, so an OCR typo or a duplicated vendor record defeats it
findings.evidence: `_duplicate_bill_id` (routers/purchase_bills.py:207-247) and migration 313's index both key on `(client_id, vendor_id, lower(btrim(bill_no)))`. Nothing compares amount or date. And `create_vendor`'s duplicate guard (routers/vendors.py:266-277) only matches on GSTIN or PAN, so two vendor rows for the same unregistered supplier are freely creatable — after which the same invoice can be booked twice under two vendor ids and neither guard fires.
findings.ca_experience: The same supplier invoice entered as 'INV-001' and 'INV 001', or scanned twice with one character misread, is booked twice: the expenditure is double-counted, the ITC is claimed twice under §16, and the deductee is filed twice on 26Q — precisely the harm the guard's own message at line 250 describes.
findings.market_standard: Dext and Zoho Books flag a possible duplicate on same-vendor + same-amount + same-date regardless of the reference; Tally warns on a repeated supplier invoice number per party per year.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a soft warning (not a refusal) when a live bill exists for the same vendor with the same `bill_date` and `total_paise` but a different number, and tighten the vendor duplicate guard to include a normalised-name match for vendors with no GSTIN or PAN.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Duplicate detection is exact-match on (client_id, vendor_id, normalised bill_no) only — apps/api/routers/purchase_bills.py:240+ and the identical partial unique index at apps/api/migrations/313_...:48-52; nothing compares amount or date. And apps/api/routers/vendors.py:267-275 only dedupes vendors on GSTIN or PAN, with no unique constraint on the table at all, so an unregistered supplier can exist twice and the same invoice can be booked under each without either guard firing. Migration 313's recorded exclusions cover cancelled/soft-deleted/blank-numbered bills, not this.
verification.probe: `grep -rn 'vendors' apps/api/migrations/*.sql | grep -i UNIQUE` -> no output (no unique index on vendors); migration 313:48-52 shows the index keyed on client_id, vendor_id, lower(btrim(bill_no)) only.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed on both halves. `_duplicate_bill_id` (apps/api/routers/purchase_bills.py:240-247 onward) keys on `(client_id, vendor_id, lower(strip(bill_no)))` and nothing else — no amount, no date — and apps/api/migrations/313_...:48-52 builds the matching partial unique index on exactly those three expressions. create_vendor's duplicate guard at apps/api/routers/vendors.py:263-275 calls _match_existing_vendor only `if gstin or pan`, and there is no unique constraint on vendors anywhere (`grep 'vendors' apps/api/migrations/*.sql | grep -i UNIQUE` -> no matches), so two rows for the same PAN-less, GSTIN-less supplier are freely creatable and the bill index then treats their invoices as distinct.
lens_notes.guards: Migration 313's header does record deliberate exclusions — cancelled bills, soft-deleted bills, blank numbers (:28-38) — but says nothing about amount/date matching or vendor duplication, so this is a residual gap rather than a decision CLAUDE.md or the migration already made. The index closes the direct-PostgREST path too (313:18-26), and tests/test_no_duplicate_purchase_bill.py pins the router check and the index together. No soft 'possible duplicate' warning exists in the Purchases page.

test_coverage_notes:
What is tested, and well: the §195 engine has 165 passing tests across tests/test_section_195_rates.py and tests/test_vendor_residency_and_27q.py covering chargeability, the treaty comparison, the two surcharge ladders, the capital-gains cap, cess on tax-plus-surcharge, and every refusal path. tests/test_no_duplicate_purchase_bill.py holds the API guard and migration 313's index together. tests/test_rule37_itc_reversal.py covers proportionate reversal, the ceiling rounding and the reversal period. tests/test_vendor_payment_concurrency.py, tests/test_purchase_payment_allocate.py and tests/test_r227_draft_bill_payment_guard.py cover the CAS and the draft-bill guard. tests/test_e2e_purchase_cycle.py walks a full lifecycle including cross-firm refusals. tests/test_itc_reversal_register.py covers the ledger-support refusal.

Two tests assert WRONG statutory behaviour, and both should be rewritten as negative controls for PUR-01 and PUR-02. tests/test_tds_bill_engine.py:59-70 (`test_h5_194c_aggregate_threshold_across_bills`) asserts `b5["tds_paise"] == 500_00` — TDS on the crossing bill alone — which under §194C(5) should be ₹2,500 on the ₹1,25,000 aggregate. tests/test_tds_bill_engine.py:43-47 (`test_h5_below_threshold_no_tds`) is correct for one ₹40,000 §194J bill in isolation, but it is the only §194J threshold test and it therefore pins a model that has no annual aggregate at all, which is where the statute puts the limit.

What has no coverage where it is computed: `is_reverse_charge` never appears in any purchase-cycle test file (grep across tests/*.py matches only GST-side files), so the branch that decides whether Trade Payables includes GST the vendor never charged is untested. `itc_eligible` never appears in a test of `_compute_bill_lines_and_totals` — only in the schema guard and the GST computer's own tests. There is no test at all for `POST /purchase-bills/from-document` (grep finds it only in tests/test_r237_ar_ap_hardening.py, which is about ageing). No test asserts that the TDS register's `statutory_gaps` reach the frontend — the payroll equivalent has one (apps/web/scripts/payroll-gaps-reach-the-screen.test.ts) and could be copied. tests/test_documents_locked_by_filed_return.py covers the purchase-bill EDIT path only (line 189), not create and not receive, which is exactly where the lock is missing. §194Q has no test anywhere. And nothing pins the GL `gst_input` movement against the GSTR-3B `books_itc` for a bill with a blocked line — that parity test would have caught PUR-04 the day it was written.
open_questions_for_owner: PUR-01 and PUR-02 are wrong money on a live path and everything else in this list is downstream of them. Do you want the FY-aggregate rewrite of the resident TDS thresholds treated as a hotfix ahead of the other findings, and do you want the two tests that currently pin the wrong §194C number rewritten as the negative control in the same commit?

On PUR-03 (surcharge and cess added on top of a DTAA rate): the module already makes and documents a conservative over-deduction choice for the §206AA floor. Is the treaty behaviour the same deliberate choice — in which case it needs a docstring and a test naming it — or is it an oversight that should be capped at the treaty rate the way most Indian practice does?

PUR-11 (2A/2B invoice-level matching against the purchase bills the product already holds) is the largest single piece of work here and, in my reading of the market, the strongest reason a CA would buy a purchase module at all. Is that the next big build, or is the GST subsystem's owner already scoping it — I stopped at the purchase-side boundary and did not audit the GST workspace.

PUR-10 asks whether TDS on advance payments is in scope.
